Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound recruiter-themed job-interview phish linking to Salesforce/exct.net → wiseagent redirect infra · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound recruiter-themed job-interview phish linking to Salesforce/exct.net → wiseagent redirect infra AIDelivery High
Hunts delivered inbound mail impersonating brand recruiters (marketing-role lure) whose links resolve to the campaign's abused redirect infrastructure (exct.net / wiseagent.com) or the adidas-hiring.com lookalike landing page. Article-specific because it pairs the recruiter/interview lure vocabulary with the exact laundering domains Will Thomas documented, not generic phishing.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources

let PhishDomains = dynamic(["adidas-hiring.com","wiseagent.com"]);

| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

| where UrlDomain in~ (PhishDomains) or (UrlDomain endswith "exct.net" and Subject has_any ("interview","recruiter","marketing role","hiring","schedule a call","opportunity"))
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction

let LookbackDays = 14d;
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["adidas-hiring.com","wiseagent.com"]);
EmailEvents

| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware

BleepingComputer
2026-07-06 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams voice calls by impersonating corporate IT support staff to trick employees into installing the EtherRAT malware, giving attackers initial access to corporate networks. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1566 T1566.001

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window · [LLM] Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound Microsoft Teams external-access chat/message activity from a foreign M365 tenant whose account poses as IT support (e.g. helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com). This is the initial-access lure in the EtherRAT vishing campaign where the 'External unfamiliar' Teams contact precedes a remote-control request. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete external-tenant IOC (helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com) plus the 'External unfamiliar' impersonation pattern; ExternalAccess==true on Teams from an onmicrosoft.com sender posing as helpdesk is the campaign's exact entry signal. Datadog/Falcon left empty — Teams audit isn't in FDR or Datadog's listed Azure sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/18/crosstenant-helpdesk-impersonation-data-exfiltration-human-operated-intrusion-playbook/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/10/07/disrupting-threats-targeting-microsoft-teams/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate managed-service-provider (MSP) helpdesk that operates from its own M365 tenant and contacts staff via external Teams
  • Partner/vendor IT collaborating cross-tenant during a genuine support case
  • Internal 'helpdesk' shared mailbox federated as a guest in a subsidiary tenant
  • Approved outsourced service-desk display names containing 'IT Support'
Suppression filter
| where UPN !has_any ("contoso-msp", "trusted-partner")  // append approved partner onmicrosoft tenants
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the sender tenant (onmicrosoft.com domain) is not an approved partner; check whether the recipient accepted a screen-share/remote-control request in the same Teams session and whether any download followed. Step 2 (contain): Block the external tenant/domain in Teams external-access policy, disable the impacted user's active sessions, and quarantine the endpoint if remote-control was granted. Step 3 (hunt): On the recipient's device pivot to RMM installs (hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe) and msiexec pulling from camorreado.click within the following hour.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application =~ "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesListed")
| extend UPN = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| where UPN has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UPN has "Progressive936" or tolower(AccountDisplayName) has_any ("helpdesk","help desk","it support","system administrator") or tolower(UPN) has "helpdesk"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, UPN, IPAddress, AccountType, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "MicrosoftTeams"
| where ExternalAccess == true
| where Operation in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesExported")
| where UserId has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UserId has "Progressive936" or tolower(UserId) has "helpdesk" or tolower(UserId) has "it-support"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, OfficeId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity` Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation IN ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent") ExternalAccess=true
| search (UserId="*Progressive936*" OR UserId="*helpdesk*" OR UserId="*it-support*" OR UserId="*helpdesk@*.onmicrosoft.com")
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count, values(Operation) as operations, values(ClientIP) as srcIPs by UserId
| sort - firstSeen
Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window AICommand & Control High
Hunts a host that executes BOTH HopToDesk and AnyDesk within a short window — the exact dual-RMM staging the attacker walks the victim through after the Teams remote-control grant. Two distinct remote-access tools appearing together on one endpoint is far higher fidelity than either tool alone. Rationale: Uses the two specific RMM binaries named in the article (HopToDesk, AnyDesk) and requires BOTH on the same host — the dcount>=2 requirement suppresses the common single-legit-AnyDesk noise while capturing the attacker's exact staging step. Datadog rule groups by host and thresholds distinctTools at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department evaluating/migrating between two RMM products on a test machine
  • Managed-service provider that legitimately deploys AnyDesk while a user separately installed HopToDesk for personal use
  • Sysadmin bench machine used to reproduce customer support scenarios with multiple remote tools
  • Security team detonating RMM samples in a sandboxed but Defender-onboarded host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("it-bench01","soc-detonation01")  // exclude sanctioned RMM-eval hosts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm neither tool is on the org's approved RMM allowlist and check for a preceding external Teams contact (UC1) or msiexec pull from camorreado.click on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Kill hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe, terminate their unattended-access sessions, and isolate the endpoint from the network. Step 3 (hunt): Look for msiexec executing v#.msi from camorreado.click and node.exe beaconing that follows the RMM sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(tolower(FileName)), Tools = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName
| where DistinctTools >= 2   // HopToDesk + AnyDesk together on one host
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend Bin = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where Bin in ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(Bin), Tools = make_set(Bin), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SampleCmd = any(CommandLine) by Computer, SubjectUserName
| where DistinctTools >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\hoptodesk.exe OR *\\HopToDesk.exe OR *\\anydesk.exe OR *\\AnyDesk.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(hoptodesk|anydesk)\.exe$/i
| RmmTool := if(ImageFileName=/hoptodesk\.exe$/i, then="hoptodesk", else="anydesk")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=RmmTool, distinct=true, as=distinctTools), collect([RmmTool])])
| distinctTools>=2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe invoked against a remote MSI hosted on camorreado[.]click (observed as v7.msi from an open directory of v1–v9 installers). This MSI is the EtherRAT loader that fetches a legit Node.js runtime and decrypts embedded payloads — a single-command, high-fidelity execution pivot. Rationale: Pins on the exact delivery domain camorreado[.]click and the v#.msi naming from the open-directory (v1-v9) — msiexec pulling a remote MSI from an attacker domain is inherently rare and the domain string makes FPs near-zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/etherrat-dissected-how-a-react2shell-implant-delivers-5-payloads-through-blockchain-c2
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution server that happens to name packages v7.msi (mitigated by the camorreado.click requirement, but the regex alone could match)
  • Developer testing a locally hosted MSI over http with a v#.msi filename
  • Legitimate vendor MSI download whose URL coincidentally contains a v-number pattern
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in an onboarded sandbox
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full msiexec command line and confirm the source URL is camorreado.click; check the parent process (was it a browser/RMM session started by the vishing lure?). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block camorreado.click at proxy/DNS, and collect the dropped MSI plus any node.exe artifacts for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the estate for other v1–v9 MSI names from camorreado.click and for node.exe spawned by msiexec beaconing to the same domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to camorreado[.]click — the EtherRAT loader-download and campaign C2 domain. Catches both the MSI/Node.js pull and subsequent beaconing regardless of which process (msiexec, node.exe, browser) drives the connection, complementing the msiexec process pivot. Rationale: camorreado[.]click is the article's single confirmed network IOC (corroborated by Malwarebytes' infrastructure write-up); a domain match is a clean pure-IOC detection and the Defender query surfaces the initiating process (expect msiexec.exe or node.exe) for immediate triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/URL-detonation appliance or analyst sandbox resolving the IOC on purpose
  • Web proxy or DNS-security product pre-resolving flagged domains for categorization
  • Newly-registered lookalike domain reused for benign parking after takedown
  • SOC tooling that pings known-bad domains for availability monitoring
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("10.10.20.5")  // exclude the URL-detonation sandbox resolver
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node.exe from a temp path or msiexec = high concern) and the requesting host/user. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block camorreado.click at DNS and proxy, isolate any host with a successful connection, and preserve node.exe + dropped payloads. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the follow-on EtherRAT behaviour — node.exe polling public Ethereum RPC endpoints for its C2 URL — and correlate back to the originating Teams vishing session and RMM installs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "camorreado.click"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "camorreado.click" or Name endswith ".camorreado.click"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData

OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Iran-Linked Hackers Use New Cavern C2 Framework to Target Israeli Organizations
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

16-Year-Old Linux KVM Flaw Lets Guest VMs Escape to Host on Intel and AMD x86 Systems

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A use-after-free bug in Linux's KVM hypervisor can be triggered from a guest virtual machine to corrupt the shadow-page state of the host kernel that runs it. Dubbed 'Januscape' and tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-53359, the flaw sits in the shadow MMU code that KVM shares across both Intel and AMD. The public proof-of-concept panics the host; the researcher claims that a separate, unreleased exploit

Unpatched x86 KVM host exposed to Januscape guest-to-host escape (CVE-2026-53359) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces Linux hosts still carrying the vulnerable KVM shadow-MMU code (kernels older than the July 4 2026 stable fixes / missing commit 81ccda30b4e8) so they can be prioritised for patching before a rented guest with nested virtualization can panic or escape to the host. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE and the shipped fixed versions. Rationale: Pins the concrete CVE-2026-53359 and the fixed stable trains (7.1.3 / 6.18.38 / 6.12.95 / 6.6.144 / 6.1.177 / 5.15.211 / 5.10.260, commit 81ccda30b4e8) named in the article; a TVM CVE lookup is exact and low-noise. Distro backports may carry the fix under a different version so the recommended-update field must be checked rather than uname alone. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://git.almalinux.org/rpms/kernel/commit/5ff608da797cb293d172082b5f4fffbcbd9b55a2
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host was patched via distro backport that keeps an old-looking version string, so it appears vulnerable but is not (check package changelog / RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
  • TVM has not yet catalogued CVE-2026-53359 (NVD unscored at disclosure) so the query returns empty on hosts that are actually exposed
  • Linux appliance images where the kernel is vendor-frozen and TVM reports the base OS version, not the running kernel
  • Hosts that expose no nested virtualization (kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0) are technically vulnerable in code but not reachable by untrusted guests
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate != "" and VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("Critical","High","Medium")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually runs KVM and accepts multi-tenant/untrusted guests, and check whether nested virtualization is enabled (cat /sys/module/kvm_intel/parameters/nested or kvm_amd) — only nested-exposed hosts are reachable. 2) Contain: if patching cannot happen immediately, set kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0 to remove the guest-reachable path, and restrict /dev/kvm permissions on RHEL-like hosts where it is world-writable (0666). 3) Hunt: verify the running kernel includes commit 81ccda30b4e8 via the package changelog, then pivot to UC 'KVM shadow-MMU host panic' on the same hosts to check for exploitation attempts.

KVM shadow-MMU use-after-free host panic (Januscape PoC signature) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the observable of the public Januscape proof-of-concept: a guest-triggered use-after-free / KASAN report or kernel panic whose stack localises to KVM shadow-MMU code (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp) on the host. A single guest can knock over the whole hypervisor and every co-tenant VM, so this is a high-priority DoS/exploitation signal. Rationale: The article and PoC state the public exploit reliably panics the host with the crash localised to the shadow MMU and names the fixed function kvm_mmu_get_child_sp; a KASAN/UAF or kernel-panic syslog line co-occurring with 'kvm' is high-fidelity for an exploitation attempt. Defender/Falcon left empty because host kernel-panic telemetry is not shipped by Defender XDR or the FDR event schema — this signal lives in host syslog/dmesg (Sentinel Syslog, Datadog linux.syslog). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://lowendtalk.com/discussion/218905/januscape-guest-to-host-escape-in-kvm-x86-cve-2026-53359
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine (non-malicious) KVM bug or hardware fault producing a kvm-related oops after a kernel upgrade
  • KASAN/lockdep debug kernels in a QA/dev fleet that log verbose 'BUG:'/'use-after-free' traces routinely
  • Memory-pressure OOM or ECC/hardware GPF that happens to include kvm frames on the stack
  • Security researchers or internal red team running the Januscape PoC in an authorised lab
Suppression filter
| where SeverityLevel in ("error","crit","alert","emerg") or SyslogMessage has_any ("use-after-free","kvm_mmu_get_child_sp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full dmesg/journal around the event, confirm the faulting stack references KVM MMU frames (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp / __kvm_mmu_get_shadow_page) rather than an unrelated subsystem, and identify which guest was running at the time. 2) Contain: cordon the hypervisor, live-migrate or isolate co-tenant VMs, and quarantine the suspect guest instance; if the host is unpatched, disable nested virtualization fleet-wide as an emergency control. 3) Hunt: cross-reference UC 'Unpatched x86 KVM host' to confirm the host lacked commit 81ccda30b4e8, and check the suspect guest for a recently loaded out-of-tree kernel module (UC 'Out-of-tree kernel module load on KVM host/guest').
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("kern","kernel")
| where SyslogMessage has "kvm"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("use-after-free","KASAN","kvm_mmu_get_child_sp","Kernel panic - not syncing","general protection fault","BUG: unable to handle")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Out-of-tree kernel module load on KVM host/guest (Januscape exploit prerequisite) AIInstallation Low
Hunts the concrete prerequisite the article states for the public PoC — a loadable kernel module — by flagging insmod/modprobe of a .ko that lives outside /lib/modules or a kernel taint message indicating an unsigned/out-of-tree module. On production hypervisors and hardened guest images, loading a custom module is rare and is the vehicle used to reach the vulnerable nested-virtualization path. Rationale: The article states the public PoC 'demonstrates a reliable host panic from a guest with a loadable kernel module', and the module is a custom .ko (not a distro-signed module under /lib/modules), which is exactly what trips the kernel taint messages matched here. Low confidence / high FP by design — scoped to modules outside /lib/modules to strip routine distro module loads. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DKMS rebuilding third-party modules (NVIDIA/CUDA, ZFS, VirtualBox guest additions) into build dirs before install
  • EDR/backup/observability agents that ship their own out-of-tree .ko (e.g. filesystem or eBPF helper modules)
  • Kernel developers or CI pipelines insmod'ing freshly built modules from a source tree
  • Hardware vendor driver installers loading a .ko from /tmp during setup
  • Container/virtualization tooling loading helper modules from non-standard paths
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nvidia","zfs","vboxguest","vboxsf","dkms","falcon","crowdstrike") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dkms","akmods","dracut"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the .ko path and hash, the loading user, and whether the module is signed; confirm whether the host is a KVM hypervisor or a rented/untrusted guest. 2) Contain: if the module is unsigned/unknown and the host is multi-tenant KVM, isolate the instance and capture memory before reboot; rmmod is unsafe if exploitation is in progress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'KVM shadow-MMU host panic' for a co-occurring crash and to UC 'Unpatched x86 KVM host' to confirm exposure; sweep the fleet for the same .ko hash/name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("insmod","modprobe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ko"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "/lib/modules/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("kern","kernel")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("loading out-of-tree module taints kernel","module verification failed: signature and/or required key missing","loading test module taints kernel")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Threat Actors Probe Gitea Docker Flaw CVE-2026-20896 13 Days After Disclosure

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a recently patched critical security flaw in Gitea Docker images, according to Sysdig. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-20896 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that stems from the DevOps platform trusting the "X-WEBAUTH-USER" header from any source IP address, effectively allowing an unauthenticated internet client to get elevated

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gitea CVE-2026-20896 auth bypass: X-WEBAUTH-USER header from untrusted source AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Gitea instance carrying the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any non-loopback / non-trusted-proxy source IP. This is the exact single-header exploit for CVE-2026-20896, where the Docker image's REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=* default lets any client impersonate any user (admin, gitea_admin) with no password or token. Rationale: Anchors on the literal exploit primitive named in the article and GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4: the X-WEBAUTH-USER header. Defender/Falcon left empty because EDR endpoint telemetry does not capture HTTP request headers; this detection lives in web/proxy/WAF logs. The loopback-exclusion in Sentinel keeps the legitimate trusted-proxy path (127.0.0.0/8) quiet. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/gitea-forgejo-nine-cves-1263-security-release-2026/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse-proxy auth (Authelia, oauth2-proxy, Cloudflare Access) genuinely injecting X-WEBAUTH-USER from the trusted loopback/proxy IP
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, internal pentest) sending the header as an exploit check
  • Load balancer or uptime health checks replaying a stored request template that includes the header
  • Internal admin testing/validating the reverse-proxy authentication configuration after patching
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full request — note the SourceIP, the X-WEBAUTH-USER value (admin/gitea_admin = high risk), and whether the request bypassed the proxy (direct hit on the container port). Confirm the Gitea build is ≤1.26.2. Step 2 (contain): If the source is external/untrusted, block the IP at the WAF/firewall, force-expire active Gitea sessions, and either set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 or upgrade to 1.26.3+. Step 3 (hunt): Review Gitea audit logs for admin actions (new SSH keys, tokens, webhooks, repo clones) tied to that session; enumerate all repos accessed since first probe; rotate any secrets/tokens the impersonated account could read.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestContext has "X-WEBAUTH-USER" or Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea CVE-2026-20896 probe source IP 159.26.98.241 (ProtonVPN) contact AIReconnaissance Medium
Alerts on any network connection to/from 159.26.98.241, the ProtonVPN egress IP Sysdig observed making the first in-the-wild probe against internet-facing Gitea instances for CVE-2026-20896. Scoped to Gitea/web-facing hosts. Rationale: Uses the single network IOC the article provides (159.26.98.241). Confidence held at Medium because it is a shared ProtonVPN egress cited only by Sysdig/THN and may be reused by benign users or rotate — hence the host-scoping and analyst-verify runbook rather than auto-block. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threat-actors-probe-gitea-docker-flaw.html • https://dailysecurityreview.com/resources/gitea-cve-2026-20896-auth-bypass-exploited-via-one-http-header/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote developer or admin browsing to Gitea over ProtonVPN sharing the same egress IP
  • Security researchers or benign internet-wide scanners (Shodan, Censys) transiting the same VPN pool
  • VPN egress reassignment over time making the IOC stale and matching unrelated traffic
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox infrastructure that replays IOCs for validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the local asset is an internet-facing Gitea/web host and check the connection direction and port — inbound to the Gitea HTTP port is the concern. Correlate with UC1 (X-WEBAUTH-USER header) for the same timeframe. Step 2 (contain): If tied to a header-bypass request or admin action, block 159.26.98.241 at the perimeter and expire Gitea sessions; if it is only a benign browse from a known dev, allowlist the user, not the IP. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 30 days of firewall/WAF logs for the same IP against all web assets, and check whether the same source attempted other Gitea endpoints (/admin, /api/v1/admin).

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "159.26.98.241" or LocalIP == "159.26.98.241"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SourceIP == "159.26.98.241" or DestinationIP == "159.26.98.241"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Gitea (≤1.26.2) exposed to CVE-2026-20896 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt surfacing hosts running Gitea versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-20896 (fixed in 1.26.3) via vulnerability-management telemetry, so they can be patched or reconfigured before the header bypass is weaponized against them. Rationale: Pins the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-20896) and patched build (1.26.3) from the article and Gitea's release blog into vulnerability-management datamodels. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because VM inventory is not expressible on their event-shaped log sources. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated dev/test Gitea instances not reachable from the internet (still worth patching but lower priority)
  • TVM keying on container image digest may mis-map or miss containerized Gitea deployments
  • Forgejo forks mis-attributed as Gitea by the scanner
  • Instances already reconfigured with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 but not yet version-upgraded (mitigated, still flagged)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each flagged host confirm the exact Gitea build and whether reverse-proxy auth (ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION) is enabled and internet-exposed. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.3+ (or 1.26.4); as an interim mitigation set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 and disable reverse-proxy auth if not required. Step 3 (hunt): For any host that was exposed, retro-hunt web/proxy logs for X-WEBAUTH-USER (UC1) and contact from 159.26.98.241 (UC2) to determine if it was probed or compromised before patching.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20896")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20896")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
