Adobe ColdFusion server process spawning OS command interpreter (CVE-2026-48282 RCE landing) AIExploitation High
Hunts the ColdFusion JVM/service (coldfusion.exe, or java.exe under a cfusion install path) spawning cmd/powershell/whoami/net/certutil etc. This is the post-RCE command-execution signal for CVE-2026-48282 exploitation, where an unauthenticated directory-traversal file-write is followed by shell commands running under the ColdFusion service account. Rationale: Pivots on the real ColdFusion service binaries (coldfusion.exe / java.exe under a cfusion path) as parent, which per Rapid7 and BleepingComputer is the exact process that spawns shells after ColdFusion RCE; parent+child pairing keeps FP low. External sources confirm CVE-2026-48282 is an arbitrary-file-write/traversal RCE. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/07/17/etr-active-exploitation-of-multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-coldfusion-flaws-exploited-in-attacks-to-drop-webshells/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ColdFusion scheduled tasks or CFML apps legitimately invoking cfexecute to run cmd/net for admin automation
  • Deployment/monitoring scripts run by the CF service account (e.g., health checks calling whoami/net)
  • ColdFusion updater/installer spawning cmd during patch application
  • Backup or AV agents that shell out under the java.exe of an unrelated app sharing a 'cfusion'-like path
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\ColdFusion2023\\cfusion\\lib\\updates","hf-updater") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "scheduletask")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line of the shell child; check whether the ColdFusion host is internet-facing and still on 2025.9/2023.20 or earlier (unpatched to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21). Correlate the spawn time against IIS/W3C request logs for a preceding traversal/write request. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process, and pull the ColdFusion service offline or block inbound 80/443 at the WAF; rotate the CF service account and datasource credentials. 3) Hunt: search for freshly written .cfm/.cfc/.jsp files under CFIDE/wwwroot (UC2), outbound C2 from the CF process, new local accounts, and reuse of the same source IP across other CF instances.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe"))
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("coldfusion","cfusion"))
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has "coldfusion.exe" or ParentProcessName has "jrunsvc.exe" or ParentProcessName has "cfexec.exe")
     or (ParentProcessName has "java.exe" and (ParentProcessName has "coldfusion" or ParentProcessName has "cfusion"))
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Webshell (.cfm/.cfc/.jsp) written into ColdFusion webroot/CFIDE by CF process (CVE-2026-48282 file write) AIInstallation High
Hunts new or modified .cfm/.cfc/.cfml/.jsp files landing under ColdFusion web roots (CFIDE, wwwroot, cf_scripts) written by the ColdFusion service process. CVE-2026-48282 is a directory-traversal arbitrary-file-write, so a CF-authored script file appearing in the webroot at runtime is the webshell-drop primitive itself. Rationale: Uses the concrete webshell landing sites named by Rapid7/BleepingComputer for ColdFusion (CFIDE, wwwroot, cf_scripts) plus CF-native script extensions, gated to writes performed by the ColdFusion process — the exact arbitrary-file-write behaviour of CVE-2026-48282 rather than a generic file-drop rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-coldfusion-flaws-exploited-in-attacks-to-drop-webshells/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/03/21/etr-rapid7-observed-exploitation-of-adobe-coldfusion/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Applying ColdFusion 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21 (the patch itself rewrites .cfm/.cfc files under cfusion)
  • Legitimate CFML application deployments / CI publishing new templates into wwwroot
  • Developers hot-editing .cfm pages on a staging CF server
  • ColdFusion Administrator regenerating cf_scripts/ajax assets after a config change
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hf-updater","\\updates\\","install.jar") or FolderPath has "\\cfusion\\lib\\updates\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped file — webshells contain <cfexecute>, cfhttp, eval, or base64 blobs and are short/obfuscated vs legitimate templates; note the write timestamp and the CF process command line. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, snapshot it for forensics, isolate the host, and take the CF instance offline until patched to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21. 3) Hunt: pivot on the file hash across all CF hosts, review IIS logs for GET/POST to that path (attacker interacting with the shell), and correlate with UC1 shell-spawn events and outbound C2.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".cfm" or FileName endswith ".cfc" or FileName endswith ".cfml" or FileName endswith ".jsp"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\CFIDE\", @"\wwwroot\", @"\cfusion\", @"\cf_scripts\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe","java.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName has_any (".cfm",".cfc",".cfml",".jsp")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\CFIDE\", @"\wwwroot\", @"\cfusion\", @"\cf_scripts\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("coldfusion.exe","java.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Directory-traversal / arbitrary-write request to ColdFusion endpoints in web logs (CVE-2026-48282 exploit attempt) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to ColdFusion paths (CFIDE, cf_scripts, .cfm/.cfc handlers) carrying directory-traversal sequences in the URI or query string. CVE-2026-48282 is exploited unauthenticated via path traversal leading to arbitrary file write, so traversal-laden requests to a CF server are the initial-access attempt on the wire. Rationale: Targets the exploit primitive KEVIntel/Watchtowr describe for CVE-2026-48282 (unauthenticated directory traversal → arbitrary file write) on the one telemetry that actually sees the inbound request: web-server/WAF logs scoped to ColdFusion URIs with traversal tokens. Left defender_kql empty because Defender AH carries no IIS request logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-adobe-coldfusion-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/adobe-patches-7-cvss-100-flaws-in.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing CF paths with traversal payloads
  • Security researchers / bug-bounty testing against the CF admin console
  • Legitimate CF apps that pass '..'-containing values in query strings (relative path params)
  • WAF already blocking the request (scStatus 403) — noise if not filtered to successful writes
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200,201,206,301,302) and cIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check scStatus — a 200/201/302 on a traversal request to a .cfm/CFIDE path is high concern; capture cIP and user-agent and geolocate (early exploitation was seen from an India-geolocated IP). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, and if the request succeeded treat the host as compromised — take CF offline and patch to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21. 3) Hunt: correlate the request time with UC2 file-write and UC1 shell-spawn on the same host, and sweep other internet-facing CF instances (Shadowserver counts ~800 exposed) for the same source IP or user-agent.

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 18 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A suspected China-nexus threat activity cluster has been observed targeting Indian taxpayers, tax professionals, and corporate finance teams to deliver a remote access trojan designed to steal sensitive data from compromised hosts. The multi-stage campaign, codenamed Operation DragonReturn by Seqrite Labs, involves sending spear-phishing emails impersonating the Income Tax Department of India.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake 'Common Offline Utility ITR' tax tool download from govtop[.]one (Operation DragonReturn delivery) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-loaded from Windows Media Player folder (DcRAT stage-2) · [LLM] DcRAT steganographic payload staged as C:\Windows\background.jpg (lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250) · [LLM] MixedSvc auto-start service persistence via 'Mixed Reality.exe' (DcRAT) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DcRAT C2 beacon to 223.26.63[.]40:2671 / exfil to kkxqbh[.]top · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fake 'Common Offline Utility ITR' tax tool download from govtop[.]one (Operation DragonReturn delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts the initial delivery stage of Operation DragonReturn: a ZIP/EXE masquerading as India's Income Tax offline filing utility (Common_Offline_Utility_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.zip / COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.exe) dropped from the govtop[.]one/incometax lure page. Article-specific because it keys on the exact cloned government utility filename and the delivery domain, not generic ZIP downloads. Rationale: Keys on the exact cloned government utility filename (Common_Offline_Utility_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27 / COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.exe) and delivery domain govtop[.]one/incometax named in the article and Seqrite blog — both are unique to this campaign, giving near-zero false positives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef987-564e-79dc-a057-8add6dd51d8e
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate taxpayer downloading the real Income Tax Department offline utility (real filename differs; the exact 'COU_ITR-1_to_4' abbreviation + .exe is the malicious variant)
  • Security researcher/analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Backup/archival tools copying an already-quarantined sample
  • EDR test files named to mimic the campaign during purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one" or FileName has "COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess (browser/mail client) and FileOriginUrl for the drop; confirm the ZIP/EXE came from govtop[.]one and hash against the Seqrite IOC list. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the ZIP/EXE and any extracted COU_ITR-*.exe, block govtop[.]one at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check the same host for a subsequent nvdaHelperRemote.dll write to C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\, a background.jpg drop in C:\Windows, and creation of the MixedSvc service.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName has_any ("Common_Offline_Utility_ITR", "COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27")
   or (FileName endswith ".zip" and FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one")
   or FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one/incometax"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "govtop.one"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-loaded from Windows Media Player folder (DcRAT stage-2) AIInstallation High
Detects the DcRAT DLL side-loading step where a 504 KB malicious nvdaHelperRemote.dll is planted in and loaded from C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\ — a masquerade of the legitimate NVDA screen-reader component. Article-specific: the legit DLL never lives under Windows Media Player, so path+name is the anomaly. Rationale: nvdaHelperRemote.dll is a legitimate NVDA screen-reader file; its presence/loading under C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\ (per the article and Seqrite process diagram) is a hard masquerade indicator unique to this DcRAT chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine NVDA install writing nvdaHelperRemote.dll — but to \Program Files\NVDA\, never Windows Media Player
  • Admin manually copying accessibility DLLs into the wrong directory (rare)
  • Software packaging tool relocating DLLs during a repackage
  • EDR/AV quarantine-restore replacing the file in its captured path
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\NVDA\" or FolderPath has @"\NVDA\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the loading process (COU_ITR-*.exe or Mixed Reality.exe) and hash of the DLL; a ~504 KB unsigned DLL under Windows Media Player is confirmation. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL and its loader, kill the loading process. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for C:\Windows\background.jpg, the MixedSvc service, and outbound to 223.26.63[.]40:2671.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nvdaHelperRemote.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows Media Player\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "nvdaHelperRemote.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has "Windows Media Player"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DcRAT steganographic payload staged as C:\Windows\background.jpg (lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250) AIInstallation High
Detects the image-based payload concealment step: the loader fetches lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250 and writes it as C:\Windows\background.jpg, from which a second-stage DLL is carved. Article-specific: a .jpg written to the Windows root by a non-system process paired with the hardcoded staging server. Rationale: C:\Windows\background.jpg written by a user-space process, plus the hardcoded staging IP 204.194.48[.]250/lllyd.jpg, are both explicit in the article and Seqrite diagram; a JPG in the Windows root is inherently anomalous and survives C2 IP rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OEM/desktop-personalization software staging a wallpaper named background.jpg (usually under \Windows\Web\Wallpaper, not the Windows root)
  • Sysadmin GPO deploying a corporate wallpaper to C:\Windows (verify the writing process is TrustedInstaller/GPO, not a user EXE)
  • Third-party theme installer dropping images
  • Imaging/MDT task-sequence writing default wallpaper during provisioning
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "svchost.exe", "msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process — if a recently-downloaded EXE (COU_ITR-*.exe / Mixed Reality.exe) wrote it, treat as confirmed; check for a preceding fetch from 204.194.48[.]250. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine background.jpg and the writing binary, block 204.194.48[.]250. 3) Hunt: look for the extracted 504 KB nvdaHelperRemote.dll under Windows Media Player and the MixedSvc service on the same and peer hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "background.jpg"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows\background.jpg"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "background.jpg"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\background.jpg"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MixedSvc auto-start service persistence via 'Mixed Reality.exe' (DcRAT) AIInstallation High
Detects the persistence step where the malware copies itself to 'Mixed Reality.exe' and registers an auto-start Windows service named MixedSvc to survive reboot. Article-specific: both the service name (MixedSvc) and the masqueraded binary name are unique to Operation DragonReturn. Rationale: Service name MixedSvc and self-copied binary 'Mixed Reality.exe' are explicitly named in the article, Seqrite blog and process diagram — a distinctive persistence signature that no legitimate software uses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Mixed Reality / WMR platform components (legit binaries are MixedRealityPortal.exe / signed by Microsoft under System32 or WindowsApps — not a bare 'Mixed Reality.exe' from a user path)
  • Developer/test service named similarly during MR app development
  • Backup agent re-registering services after restore
  • Sysadmin installing a HMD vendor driver package
Suppression filter
| where ServiceFileName !has @"\WindowsApps\" and ServiceFileName !has @"\System32\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ServiceFileName/ImagePath — a 'Mixed Reality.exe' outside System32/WindowsApps, unsigned or signed anomalously, confirms it; note the InitiatingProcess. 2) Contain: stop and delete the MixedSvc service (sc delete MixedSvc), quarantine Mixed Reality.exe, isolate host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the MixedSvc service name and for injected svchost.exe beaconing to 223.26.63[.]40:2671.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| extend SvcName = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).ServiceName), ImagePath = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).ImagePath)
| where SvcName =~ "MixedSvc" or ImagePath has "Mixed Reality.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SvcName, ImagePath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "MixedSvc" or ServiceFileName has "Mixed Reality.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DcRAT C2 beacon to 223.26.63[.]40:2671 / exfil to kkxqbh[.]top AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the DcRAT command-and-control and data-exfiltration stage: encrypted beacon to the hardcoded C2 223.26.63[.]40 on non-standard port 2671, and exfil to kkxqbh[.]top (plus related actor domains). Article/diagram-specific IP+port combination and exfil domain. Rationale: 223.26.63[.]40:2671 (the exact DcRAT C2 IP and port from the Seqrite diagram) and exfil domain kkxqbh[.]top are hard, campaign-unique IOCs; the non-standard port on the fixed IP makes this a low-FP alerting detection even against encrypted traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef987-564e-79dc-a057-8add6dd51d8e
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/scanning platforms (Shodan, Censys) probing 223.26.63[.]40 from a sanctioned scanner host
  • Analyst sandbox detonation generating the beacon deliberately
  • Stale IOC reuse if the ChinaNet IP is later reassigned to benign hosting (validate recency)
  • Security proxy/sinkhole re-resolving the exfil domains during enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process — if it is svchost.exe launched from an unusual path or injected by MixedSvc/Mixed Reality.exe, treat as confirmed DcRAT. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 223.26.63[.]40 and kkxqbh[.]top (+related domains) at firewall/DNS, kill the process and MixedSvc service. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts contacting the C2 IP/domains, then back-trace to the govtop[.]one download, nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-load and background.jpg drop to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "223.26.63.40" and RemotePort == 2671)
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "223.26.63.40" and DstPortNumber == 2671)
   or DstHostname in~ ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
   or Url has_any ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027

Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("nvdahelperremote.dll", "reality.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("C:\Windows\background.jpg."))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,

When checking the URL isn’t enough: a Device Code Phishing attack via a Microsoft website

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-06 9 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant specification was designed to streamline authentication for Smart TVs, IoT devices, and printers. Today, threat actors are weaponizing it.

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.001
Domainscacoo.com allianceinvestigators.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Law-firm / order-confirmation lure delivering device-code phish via cacoo.com and allianceinvestigators.com · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID Device Authorization Grant (device code) authentication flow sign-in · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-device-code token abuse: mailbox / OneDrive / Teams access from a new IP after device-code sign-in · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra ID Device Authorization Grant (device code) authentication flow sign-in AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (device code) flow — the exact mechanism abused in this campaign, where the attacker's server-side app fetches a user_code and the victim approves it (plus MFA) on Microsoft's legitimate page. Surfaces the users, client apps, source IPs and countries so an analyst can spot device-code auth on non-input-constrained principals (regular office users) that should never legitimately use it. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core mechanic: the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant completed on login.microsoftonline.com. Sentinel's canonical AuthenticationProtocol=='deviceCode' column is used in the Sigma rule; the Defender/Sentinel bodies pivot on the in-schema AuthenticationProcessingDetails blob plus the Microsoft Authentication Broker client app because AuthenticationProtocol is not exposed in this tenant's Advanced-Hunting/Sentinel column set. Device code auth on regular knowledge-worker accounts is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-device-code
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Teams Rooms / smart-display or conference devices that legitimately enroll via device code
  • Admins running 'az login --use-device-code' or Azure PowerShell Connect-AzAccount -UseDeviceAuthentication
  • Intune / Autopilot device enrollment through the Microsoft Authentication Broker app
  • Kiosk or signage endpoints that lack a keyboard and use device code by design
  • Developers authenticating headless CI runners with device code
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Intune", "Microsoft Intune Enrollment", "Microsoft Teams Rooms")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the AccountUpn is a device-constrained principal (Teams Room, kiosk, service). If it is a normal user, treat device-code sign-in as suspicious; check the source IP/country vs the user's baseline and whether MFA was satisfied. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions' in Entra), force password reset, and block sign-in if the IP is foreign/unexpected. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on AccountObjectId across CloudAppEvents/OfficeActivity for MailItemsAccessed, Send, inbox-rule creation, and OneDrive downloads in the following 24h; review inbound EmailEvents to the user for the law-firm / order-confirmation lure and cacoo.com / allianceinvestigators.com URLs.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName has "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize SignIns = count(), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Country, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, ClientAppUsed
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| extend Loc = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignIns = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Loc, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, ClientAppUsed
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Entra ID Device Code Authentication Flow Sign-In
id: 8f2a1c74-9b3e-4d21-bc55-2e7a4d6f9c10
description: Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (device code) flow, abused in device code phishing.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AuthenticationProtocol: 'deviceCode'
    ResultType: 0
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Smart TVs, conference-room devices and CLI tools (az login --use-device-code) that legitimately use device code flow
level: medium
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:"Microsoft Authentication Broker" @properties.status.errorCode:0
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as src_ips from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success (Authentication.signature_id="deviceCode" OR Authentication.app="Microsoft Authentication Broker") by Authentication.user Authentication.authentication_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="" | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as src_ips from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success (Authentication.signature_id="deviceCode" OR Authentication.app="Microsoft Authentication Broker") by Authentication.user Authentication.authentication_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="" | sort - lastTime
Law-firm / order-confirmation lure delivering device-code phish via cacoo.com and allianceinvestigators.com AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the inbound delivery stage of this campaign: emails styled as a law-firm notice (password-protected PDF) or a Portuguese order/quote confirmation whose links route through legitimate open-redirect infrastructure (cacoo.com) or the actor's legal-portal domain (allianceinvestigators.com) toward a device-code phishing page. Article-specific because it keys on the two confirmed IOC domains and the password-protected-PDF-with-link delivery pattern rather than generic phishing. Rationale: Uses the two article-confirmed IOC domains (cacoo.com used as an open redirect, allianceinvestigators.com as the mimicked legal portal) joined against inbound Safe-Links URL telemetry. AttachmentCount surfaces the password-protected-PDF variant. High-fidelity because these exact domains carrying inbound mail is rare and directly tied to the observed campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1566.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business use of cacoo.com (Nulab diagramming) — colleagues sharing genuine Cacoo diagram links
  • Inbound mail from a genuine partner law firm that happens to attach password-protected PDFs
  • Marketing/newsletter senders embedding cacoo.com asset links
  • Internal users legitimately corresponding with allianceinvestigators.com if it is a real vendor in your supply chain
  • Safe Links rewriting a benign cacoo.com link inside a forwarded thread
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the flagged messages; confirm the lure (law-firm notice with password-protected PDF, or Portuguese order/quote confirmation) and follow the cacoo.com / allianceinvestigators.com URL chain to see whether it terminates on a device-code / copy-the-code page. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete/quarantine matching messages tenant-wide (Threat Explorer > purge), block the sender and allianceinvestigators.com at the gateway, and add the redirect URL to the block list. Step 3 (hunt): For each recipient, check UrlClickEvents for a click-through and then pivot to UC1 (device-code sign-in) and UC3 (post-auth mailbox/OneDrive access) to determine which recipients actually authenticated.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("cacoo.com", "allianceinvestigators.com")
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("cacoo.com", "allianceinvestigators.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Post-device-code token abuse: mailbox / OneDrive / Teams access from a new IP after device-code sign-in AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a successful device-code sign-in with follow-on cloud activity (MailItemsAccessed, mail Send, inbox-rule creation, OneDrive downloads) performed on the same account from a DIFFERENT source IP within 24h — the exact post-compromise behaviour described, where the attacker used the harvested access/refresh tokens to read and send mail, exfiltrate OneDrive files and access Teams. Article-specific because it is chained to the device-code auth event rather than a generic anomalous-access rule. Rationale: Chains the device-code auth event (article's credential-theft step) to the article's stated impact — reading/sending mail, OneDrive exfiltration, Teams access — and requires a source-IP change within 24h to strip legitimate device-code roaming. The IP-mismatch + short-window join is the noise reducer that separates attacker token replay from the user's own follow-on activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/microsoft-device-code-phishing-attack/120350/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/
ATT&CKT1114 T1530 T1528
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User completes device-code auth on a kiosk then works from their laptop on a different NAT/egress IP
  • Corporate VPN or proxy rotation changing the egress IP between the auth and the activity
  • Mobile user roaming between cellular and Wi-Fi within the 24h window
  • Legitimate Teams Room / signage device auth followed by admin management from another IP
  • Outlook/OneDrive mobile client on a different carrier IP than the browser used to approve the code
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Compare AuthIP/AuthCountry with the activity IP/country; a foreign or hosting-provider (VPS) activity IP against a domestic auth is high-signal. Review which mailbox items were accessed, what was sent, and any newly created inbox rules. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, disable any attacker-created inbox/forwarding rules, reset credentials, and block the activity IP. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all messages Sent/forwarded during the window (BEC pivot), check OneDrive/SharePoint audit for bulk downloads, and sweep other users who received the same law-firm / order-confirmation lure for parallel device-code sign-ins.
let DeviceCodeAuth = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName has "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, AuthIP = IPAddress, AuthCountry = Country;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "SendAs", "FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloaded", "New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeAuth on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 24h)
| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and IPAddress != AuthIP
| project Timestamp, AuthTime, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, ActionType, Application, ActivityIP = IPAddress, ActivityCountry = CountryCode, AuthIP, AuthCountry, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeAuth = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AuthIP = IPAddress;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "SendAs", "FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloaded", "New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeAuth on $left.UserId == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 24h)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP) and ClientIP != AuthIP
| project TimeGenerated, AuthTime, UserId, Operation, OfficeWorkload, ClientIP, AuthIP, OfficeObjectId = OfficeId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

status: experimental

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

New TrojPix Attack Leaks Data From Air-Gapped Systems via Video Cable Emissions

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 5 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Shandong University&nbsp;have shown a fast new way to pull data off computers that are cut off from every network. The technique, called&nbsp;TrojPix, tweaks on-screen pixels in ways the eye cannot see, so that the video cable carrying them radiates a faint radio signal a nearby receiver can decode. But TrojPix works only once malware is already on the target machine, so it

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ImFileEvent

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Java-Based QuimaRAT MaaS Built to Run on Windows, Linux, and macOS

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 12 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a novel Java-based remote access trojan (RAT) called QuimaRAT that's capable of targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS environments. According to LevelBlue, the cross-platform malware is advertised under a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model, costing anywhere between $150 for one month to $1,200 for lifetime access. Other subscription tiers include $300 for

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1190 T1204.002 T1204.004 T1486 T1547.001 T1555.003
