Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Java payload executed from browser-download/temp path (QuimaRAT Quima Loader SmartScreen bypass) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Java runtime (java/javaw) writing a Registry Run/RunOnce autostart value (QuimaRAT persistence) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java runtime beaconing to Pastebin dead-drop for C2 host rotation (QuimaRAT) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Java payload executed from browser-download/temp path (QuimaRAT Quima Loader SmartScreen bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Quima Loader browser-cache delivery chain: a 'small clean loader' or browser saves a JAR/EXE to Downloads/Temp and a JVM (java.exe/javaw.exe) then executes it, bypassing SmartScreen. Article-specific because QuimaRAT is a Java implant delivered via HTA/LNK fake-CAPTCHA/update landing pages that stage the payload from browser cache. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete facts — Java implant (java/javaw), -jar execution, Quima Loader staging the payload into browser cache/Downloads, and SmartScreen bypass on execution. Behavior-based only; no hash/domain IOC exists to corroborate (LevelBlue is sole source). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to.html • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/07/06/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to-run-on-windows-linux-and-macos/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1553.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a self-built JAR from their Downloads/Temp folder
  • Minecraft/other game launchers executing modpack JARs from AppData
  • Enterprise Java line-of-business apps that stage JARs in %TEMP% during install
  • QA/build agents launching -jar test harnesses from working directories under Temp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("\\Program Files\\", "minecraft", "\\gradle\\", "\\.m2\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the JAR path + SHA256 from the child process; check whether the JAR was written seconds earlier by a browser/loader (DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl) and whether a fake-CAPTCHA/update landing URL preceded it in UrlClickEvents. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the source URL/domain at proxy, quarantine the JAR and any sibling loader EXE. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a java-written Run key / Startup drop and java outbound to pastebin.com (see companion UCs); sweep org for the same JAR hash and origin URL.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Temp\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Downloads\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Temp\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Java Payload Executed From Browser Download or Temp Path (QuimaRAT Quima Loader)
id: 8a2f1c74-6b3e-4d21-9a5c-1e7f0b2d4c88
description: Detects a JVM (java.exe/javaw.exe) executing a -jar payload from a Downloads/Temp/AppData path with a browser or script-host parent, matching the QuimaRAT Quima Loader browser-cache delivery and SmartScreen bypass.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1553.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '-jar'
  paths:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
      - '\Temp\'
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  condition: selection and paths and parent
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\java.exe OR *\\javaw.exe OR *\\JAVA.EXE OR *\\JAVAW.EXE) @CommandLine:*-jar* (@CommandLine:*\\Downloads\\* OR @CommandLine:*\\Temp\\* OR @CommandLine:*\\AppData\\*) @ParentImage:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\explorer.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\javaw?\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/-jar/i
| regex("(?i)\\\\(Downloads|Temp|AppData)\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|explorer|mshta|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("java.exe","javaw.exe")) AND Processes.process="*-jar*" AND (Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("java.exe","javaw.exe")) AND Processes.process="*-jar*" AND (Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Java runtime (java/javaw) writing a Registry Run/RunOnce autostart value (QuimaRAT persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts QuimaRAT's Windows persistence: the Java implant registers itself under HKCU/HKLM CurrentVersion\Run or RunOnce. A JVM directly authoring a Run-key value is rare in benign environments and is one of QuimaRAT's three stated Windows persistence methods (Run keys, Scheduled Tasks, Startup folder). Rationale: Directly encodes the article's stated persistence method (Registry Run keys) plus the Java-implant fact — a JVM as the process authoring a Run/RunOnce value is a high-fidelity, low-FP combination. RegistryValueData surfaces the java -jar command for triage without needing a known value name. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to.html • https://www.infosectoday.io/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to-run-on-windows-linux-and-macos/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java auto-updater (e.g. Oracle/Adoptium) writing a scheduled-update entry — usually via javaws/jusched, not javaw, but check
  • Enterprise Java desktop app installers registering a launch-on-logon entry
  • Home-grown Java utility that self-registers autostart on first run
  • Software-packaging/SCCM job invoking java to set an autostart during deployment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("\\Program Files\\Java\\", "\\Program Files (x86)\\Java\\", "jusched", "javaws") and RegistryValueData !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData/RegistryValueName — a value pointing at a -jar in Downloads/Temp/AppData or an unsigned JAR is malicious; a Program Files path from a known vendor JRE updater is likely benign. 2) Contain: delete the autostart value, isolate host, quarantine the referenced JAR. 3) Hunt: correlate with the delivery UC (java from Downloads) and the Pastebin C2 UC on the same DeviceId; also check Scheduled Tasks and the Startup folder for a sibling java persistence entry.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Java runtime beaconing to Pastebin dead-drop for C2 host rotation (QuimaRAT) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts QuimaRAT's optional Pastebin-based C2 host-update mechanism: the Java implant resolves its live C2 by fetching a Pastebin paste. Detects java.exe/javaw.exe making a DNS/network request to pastebin.com — a JVM contacting Pastebin is a strong dead-drop-resolver signal. Rationale: Encodes two named article facts — the Java implant and the Pastebin C2 host-update mechanism — into a process-attributed network/DNS pivot. A JVM resolving pastebin is rare enough to hunt on. No specific paste URL is published, so the domain is the tightest available anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to.html • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/07/06/new-java-based-quimarat-maas-built-to-run-on-windows-linux-and-macos/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/CI Java tooling pulling a Gist/paste for config or snippet retrieval
  • Java-based script that legitimately fetches text from pastebin.com
  • Security-research or sandbox VM where an analyst manually fetches pastes via a Java tool
  • Java updater or plugin that mirrors release notes from a paste service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("\\Program Files\\Java\\", "\\gradle\\", "\\.m2\\", "jenkins", "maven")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full pastebin URL/paste ID from proxy/Zeek and the java command line; a raw paste containing an IP:port or base64 config confirms dead-drop use. 2) Contain: block the paste URL and any C2 host it referenced, isolate the host, capture the java process memory before kill. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for java Run-key persistence and the browser-delivered JAR; extract the decoded C2 host from the paste and sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for connections to it.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("pastebin.com","pastebin.pl") or RemoteUrl endswith "pastebin.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("pastebin.com","pastebin.pl") or RemoteUrl endswith "pastebin.com"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

Opera GX Flaw Let Malicious Sites Auto-Install Mods to Steal Data From Visited Pages

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers found a flaw in&nbsp;Opera GX, the gaming-focused version of the Opera browser, that let a malicious website silently install a browser add-on and use it to lift specific data from the pages a victim visits. In a proof of concept, they reconstructed a signed-in user's full Gmail address from a single visit, with no click. Opera has patched the flaw and says it found no evidence that

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Silent Opera GX mod (.crx) written by browser from a non-Opera origin
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Opera GX below patched build 130.0.5847.89 (silent mod-install / universal CSS injection exposure)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Opera GX background-image request burst to a single host (universal CSS injection XS-Leak exfil) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Opera GX below patched build 130.0.5847.89 (silent mod-install / universal CSS injection exposure) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints running a version of Opera GX older than 130.0.5847.89, the build that fixed the zero-click GX Mods auto-install flaw enabling universal CSS injection and XS-Leak data theft. This is the exposure/attack-surface hunt for the specific vulnerable browser named in the article; there is no CVE, so the fixed version string is the only reliable pivot. Rationale: Uses the article's exact patched build 130.0.5847.89 as a deterministic version boundary; parse_version() gives a correct numeric comparison rather than a fragile string match. Cross-checked the version/patch claim against Infosecurity Magazine and CyberPress. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/opera-gx-flaw-gx-mods-css/ • https://cyberpress.org/opera-gx-universal-css-injection-flaw/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-opera-gx-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1176
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Opera GX beta/developer channel builds that carry a differently-formatted version string TVM cannot parse
  • A managed fleet mid-rollout where the update has been staged but not yet applied on reboot
  • Kiosk/lab machines intentionally pinned to an older browser build
  • TVM inventory lag showing a version that was already updated hours ago
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion at opera://about on a sample host; TVM can lag a reboot behind reality. 2) Contain: push Opera GX auto-update or an org-managed reinstall to 130.0.5847.89+; where update can't be forced, temporarily restrict Opera GX via app control on high-value/executive endpoints. 3) Hunt: for any host that was vulnerable, pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceId to check whether a .crx mod was silently written or a background-image request burst occurred while the browser was open.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName contains "Opera GX" or (SoftwareVendor has "Opera" and SoftwareName has "GX")
| where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
| extend Ver = parse_version(SoftwareVersion), Fixed = parse_version("130.0.5847.89")   // build that patched the GX Mods auto-install flaw
| where Ver < Fixed
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
Silent Opera GX mod (.crx) written by browser from a non-Opera origin AIDelivery Medium
Detects Opera GX (opera.exe) writing a .crx mod file into its Opera GX profile/Extensions path where the download origin/referrer is NOT an Opera domain. Legitimate GX mods install from Opera's own mods store; a .crx auto-installed via a hidden iframe on an arbitrary site is exactly the zero-click delivery step the article describes. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete artifacts: the .crx mod format, the opera.exe writer, the Opera GX profile path, and the origin-not-from-Opera discriminator that separates a store install from an iframe drive-by. FileOriginUrl/Referrer is the high-fidelity element; the Sigma/Sysmon path lacks origin, so it flags all opera .crx writes (noisier but portable). Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/opera-gx-flaw-gx-mods-css/ • https://github.com/opera-gaming/gxmods • https://cyberpress.org/opera-gx-universal-css-injection-flaw/
ATT&CKT1176 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately drag-and-drop installing a GX mod .crx downloaded from a third-party mod site or GitHub
  • Developer sideloading an unpacked/packed extension for testing via opera://extensions
  • Sync/roaming-profile tooling copying an existing Extensions directory that contains a .crx
  • A .crx cached with an empty FileOriginUrl (silent install) that the Defender query still flags but analysts must manually attribute
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Temp\\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl — a referrer that is an arbitrary unrelated website (not addons.opera.com / opera.com) plus no user download prompt strongly indicates the iframe auto-install. Check whether the mod notification bar was dismissed. 2) Contain: remove the mod (opera://extensions or delete the Extensions subfolder), block the origin/referrer domain at proxy, and force-update the browser to 130.0.5847.89+. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user, run UC3 for a background-image request burst to a single external host in the seconds after the .crx write, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for a scripted redirect to myaccount.google.com right after the install.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".crx"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "opera.exe"
| where FolderPath has "Opera GX" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Opera GX"
| where not((FileOriginUrl has "opera.com") or (FileOriginReferrerUrl has "opera.com"))   // legit GX mods come from Opera's own store/CDN
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "crx" or TargetFileName endswith ".crx"
| where ActingProcessName has "opera.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has "Opera GX"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Silent Opera GX Mod (.crx) Written by Opera Browser Process
id: 7f3c1e94-2a6b-4d18-9c0a-3e5b8d21af44
status: experimental
description: Opera GX writing a .crx mod file into its Opera GX profile path, the delivery step of the zero-click GX Mods auto-install universal CSS injection flaw.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/opera-gx-flaw-let-malicious-sites-auto.html
  - https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/opera-gx-flaw-gx-mods-css/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06

  product: windows

#event_simpleName=FileWritten

| regex("Opera.?GX", field=ContextImageFileName)

Opera GX background-image request burst to a single host (universal CSS injection XS-Leak exfil) AIActions on Objectives Low
Detects Opera GX (opera.exe) firing an abnormal burst of outbound requests to one external host in a short window — the observable signature of the mod's universal CSS injection leaking a value character-by-character via attribute-selector background-image fetches to the attacker's collection server. Targets the actual data-theft phase (the PoC reconstructed a Gmail address on myaccount.google.com). Rationale: The universal CSS injection leaks data as a burst of background-image GETs to the attacker's server, distinct from the page the user is on — so opera.exe → many rapid connections to one public host is the closest endpoint-observable of the exfil. Threshold-based and CDN-heavy, hence Low confidence / high FP; Sentinel omitted because standard tenant network telemetry lacks per-process (opera.exe) attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/opera-gx-flaw-gx-mods-css/ • https://cyberpress.org/opera-gx-universal-css-injection-flaw/
ATT&CKT1176 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A media-rich or ad-heavy site legitimately loading dozens of images/resources from one CDN in a minute
  • Streaming/live-tile GX features pulling many assets from Opera's own CDN
  • Large web-app initial load (maps, image galleries) exceeding the 30/min threshold
  • Browser prefetch/speculative connections to a single origin
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("google.com","gstatic.com","googleusercontent.com","cloudflare.com","akamai","akamaihd.net","fastly","doubleclick.net","opera.com","operacdn.com","cdn.jsdelivr.net")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the destination host — a burst to a domain unrelated to any tab the user opened, especially right after a redirect to myaccount.google.com, is the tell; benign CDNs (gstatic, cloudflare, doubleclick) are the usual noise. 2) Contain: block the destination host at proxy/firewall, remove any recently-installed GX mod (see UC2), and update the browser. 3) Hunt: correlate the burst window with a UC2 .crx write on the same DeviceId and any scripted navigation to Google/other credential-bearing account pages; sweep other hosts hitting the same destination host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "opera.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Opera GX"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","HttpConnectionInspected")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where ConnCount > 30   // burst of attribute-selector background-image fetches from the mod CSS to one attacker host in <=1 min
| order by ConnCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "opera.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Opera GX"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","HttpConnectionInspected")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where ConnCount > 30   // burst of attribute-selector background-image fetches from the mod CSS to one attacker host in <=1 min
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*Opera?GX*\\opera.exe OR *Opera?GX*\\Opera.exe OR *Opera?GX*\\OPERA.EXE)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/opera\.exe$/i
| regex("Opera.?GX", field=ContextImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
| _count>30
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app="opera.exe" All_Traffic.direction=outbound by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where count > 30
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app="opera.exe" All_Traffic.direction=outbound by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a

AI coding-agent detonates payload from scanner-skipped .git/ directory (SkillCloak SFS packing) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the SkillCloak self-extracting-skill (SFS) packing technique where a malicious agent skill hides its payload in a directory static scanners skip (.git/) and rebuilds/executes it only at runtime. Fires when a coding agent (Claude Code/node, Codex/python) or a shell it spawns executes a script or binary whose path sits inside a .git/ tree — behaviour legitimate tooling almost never exhibits outside git hooks. Rationale: Anchors on the two verbatim code-block strings from the article (.git/ and build/) as the SFS packing hide-spot, scoped to the article's named agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenClaw). Execution from inside a .git/ tree is near-zero in benign use outside git hooks, so it is a high-fidelity 'detonation' signal. Cross-checked arxiv 2607.02357 and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02357 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-skillcloak-technique-lets-malicious.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/agent-skill-malware-targets-claude-code-and-openai-codex/amp/
ATT&CKT1027 T1195.001 T1564
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Git hooks (pre-commit, post-checkout) legitimately executing scripts from .git/hooks/
  • Developer tooling that stores worktree metadata or LFS smudge/clean filters under .git/
  • Build systems that cache or vendor scripts inside a .git submodule path
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) invoking git-internal helper scripts
  • Custom CI runners that place ephemeral scripts inside a checked-out .git directory
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\.git\hooks\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\.git\hooks\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm the parent is a coding agent and the executed file lives in .git/ but is NOT a standard git hook; hash the child binary/script and check reputation. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, isolate the host, and quarantine the offending skill/repo directory before it re-detonates on next agent run. 3) Hunt: sweep the same user/host for other agent skills, look for outbound connections from the detonated child, and check for the DNS-TXT fetch and secret-env access described in the sibling UCs.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FolderPath has @"\.git\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\.git\" or ProcessCommandLine has "/.git/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Code Execution From Git Internal Directory By AI Coding Agent
id: 2b7e4c1a-9d3f-4c22-8a41-5e6f0a1c9d21
description: Detects a coding agent or a shell it spawns executing a file located inside a .git/ tree, matching SkillCloak self-extracting-skill packing that hides payloads in scanner-skipped directories.
references:

Poisoned-repo runtime payload fetch via DNS TXT record by AI coding agent (0DIN axiom chain) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Mozilla 0DIN poisoned-repository chain where a clean-looking package (demo name 'axiom') refuses to run until the agent executes an init step (python3 -m axiom init) that pulls executable content from an attacker-controlled DNS TXT record — so no malicious code is ever in the repo for a static scan to catch. Fires on a coding agent or its child issuing a TXT-type DNS lookup or the axiom init string, the runtime-fetch primitive the SkillCloak article cites as the same static-scan blind spot. Rationale: Uses the corroborated 0DIN chain specifics (python3 -m axiom init, RuntimeError-driven init, payload pulled from a DNS TXT record and executed) that THN cites as the same runtime-fetch blind spot SkillCloak exploits. A coding-agent context issuing a TXT-type lookup is rare and the Falcon DnsRequest RequestType=TXT pivot is especially clean. Cross-checked Tom's Hardware/0DIN and cyberpress. Cross-checked against: • https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/cyber-security/ai-coding-agents-can-be-tricked-into-installing-malware-via-clean-github-repositories-mozillas-0din-team-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-exploited-by-its-own-helpfulness • https://cyberpress.org/claude-code-dns-txt-payload/ • https://aiweekly.co/alerts/0din-clean-github-repos-can-trick-ai-agents-into-reverse-shells
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SPF/DKIM/DMARC or ACME dns-01 tooling that queries TXT records from a script
  • Developers manually running nslookup -type=txt / dig txt while troubleshooting DNS
  • Cloud SDKs resolving TXT-based service discovery records
  • Package managers verifying domain ownership via TXT during publish
  • A real project actually named/aliased 'axiom' with a benign init subcommand
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process spawned immediately after the TXT lookup and the resolved TXT record contents (Falcon DnsRequest / DNS resolver logs) — benign TXT queries are not followed by shell/interpreter execution of the response. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN and any AWS keys exported into that shell, and remove the poisoned repo/package. 3) Hunt: pivot on the queried domain across all hosts, look for the reverse-shell egress in the sibling secret-exfil UC, and review recently cloned repos with 'init'-style setup instructions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "axiom init"

title: AI Coding Agent Retrieves Runtime Payload Via DNS TXT Record
id: 6d1f2a83-4b7c-49e0-9f2a-1c3d5e7b8a90
description: Detects a coding agent or its child process performing a TXT-type DNS lookup or the 0DIN axiom init step used to fetch and execute a payload from an attacker-controlled DNS TXT record at runtime.
references:
  - https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/cyber-security/ai-coding-agents-can-be-tricked-into-installing-malware-via-clean-github-repositories-mozillas-0din-team-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-exploited-by-its-own-helpfulness
  - https://cyberpress.org/claude-code-dns-txt-payload/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1071.004
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\claude.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\codex.exe'
      - '\openclaw.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
  selection_axiom:
    CommandLine|contains: 'axiom init'
  selection_nslookup:
    Image|endswith: '\nslookup.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-type=txt'
      - '-q=txt'
      - '-querytype=txt'
  selection_psdns:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'Resolve-DnsName'
      - 'TXT'
  condition: selection_parent and (selection_axiom or selection_nslookup or selection_psdns)
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\claude.exe OR *\codex.exe OR *\openclaw.exe OR *\bash.exe) (@CommandLine:*axiom\ init* OR (@Image:(*\nslookup.exe OR *\NSLOOKUP.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*-type=txt* OR *-q=txt* OR *-querytype=txt*)) OR (@CommandLine:*Resolve-DnsName* AND @CommandLine:*TXT*))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest RequestType="TXT"
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|claude|python|python3|codex|openclaw|bash|sh)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*axiom init*" OR (Processes.process_name="nslookup.exe" AND (Processes.process="*-type=txt*" OR Processes.process="*-q=txt*" OR Processes.process="*-querytype=txt*")) OR (Processes.process="*Resolve-DnsName*" AND Processes.process="*TXT*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("dig","dig.exe") AND Processes.process="*txt*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*axiom init*" OR (Processes.process_name="nslookup.exe" AND (Processes.process="*-type=txt*" OR Processes.process="*-q=txt*" OR Processes.process="*-querytype=txt*")) OR (Processes.process="*Resolve-DnsName*" AND Processes.process="*TXT*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("dig","dig.exe") AND Processes.process="*txt*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
AI coding agent spawns reverse shell referencing cloud/AI secret env vars AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the payoff stage of the 0DIN poisoned-repo / malicious-skill chain: a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) spawns a shell or netcat that either carries reverse-shell primitives or reads the exact secrets 0DIN flagged as targets (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN). This is the credential-theft/backdoor outcome the SkillCloak article warns runs with the agent's own access. Rationale: Combines the article's core warning (a bad skill runs with the agent's access to steal credentials/install a backdoor) with the exact secret names 0DIN enumerated as targets (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN) plus canonical reverse-shell primitives. Coding agent parent + shell child + secret/reverse-shell intent is a high-fidelity three-part combination, not bare shell noise. Cross-checked against: • https://aiweekly.co/alerts/0din-clean-github-repos-can-trick-ai-agents-into-reverse-shells • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-skillcloak-technique-lets-malicious.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-claude-code-attack/
ATT&CKT1552 T1059.004 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate skill/setup scripts that echo or export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/GITHUB_TOKEN for authenticated operations
  • Developer debugging shells printing environment for troubleshooting
  • CI-style tasks the agent runs that pass GITHUB_TOKEN to gh/git over HTTPS (not a socket)
  • Admins using nc/ncat for benign connectivity tests from a terminal the agent launched
  • PowerShell modules that instantiate Net.Sockets.TCPClient for legitimate service checks
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GITHUB_TOKEN") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://","git ","gh ") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("/dev/tcp/","Net.Sockets.TCPClient","socket.socket","-e /bin/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and the remote endpoint/port — distinguish a secret being passed to a legitimate HTTPS git/gh call from a raw socket or /dev/tcp reverse shell; confirm the parent coding agent and the originating repo/skill. 2) Contain: kill the shell + agent, isolate the host, and immediately rotate ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN, and AWS keys exposed in that session. 3) Hunt: correlate with the DNS-TXT fetch and .git/ detonation sibling UCs on the same host, enumerate other installed agent skills, and search egress logs for the reverse-shell destination across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("bash.exe","sh.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","nc.exe","ncat.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY","GITHUB_TOKEN","/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","Net.Sockets.TCPClient","socket.socket")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","claude.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","codex.exe","openclaw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("bash.exe","sh.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","nc.exe","ncat.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY","GITHUB_TOKEN","/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","Net.Sockets.TCPClient","socket.socket")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7") or SHA1 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7") or MD5 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7") or SHA1 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7") or MD5 in~ ("818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d", "f4e41aa269c88bf11a2022701a9cf41e9a186aa1b224d837c31bf34e0b875d0e", "881ce5cb124c4d2e814783724cc1388f6a1cbf6eee274c3f3366e77ba3503ad7"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JadePuffer ransomware used AI agent to automate entire attack

BleepingComputer

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CVE-2025-3248 Langflow exploit — POST to /api/v1/validate/code
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow server process spawning shell/credential-recon after CVE-2025-3248 RCE · [LLM] Nacos CVE-2021-29441 auth bypass — rogue admin creation via Nacos-Server UA
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cron persistence written by a web-server process (JadePuffer 30-min beacon) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JadePuffer C2 beaconing to 45.131.66.106 / 64.20.53.230 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Nacos database ransomware — AES_ENCRYPT + config_info drop + README_RANSOM table · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow server process spawning shell/credential-recon after CVE-2025-3248 RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the JadePuffer Langflow exploit: the Langflow/uvicorn Python process spawning shell, transfer, or credential-harvesting commands (env dumps, /proc/self/environ, cloud/AI API-key strings). A web-app server process spawning /bin/sh or grepping for OPENAI/ANTHROPIC keys is not normal application behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the Langflow/uvicorn parent (the CVE-2025-3248 exec() sink runs in-process) spawning shell/transfer binaries or grepping the AI/cloud API keys Sysdig lists as JadePuffer's recon targets. Web-server-process-to-shell is inherently anomalous, keeping FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/jadepuffer-agentic-ransomware-for-automated-database-extortion • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/cve-2025-3248-rce-vulnerability-langflow • https://www.offsec.com/blog/cve-2025-3248/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-3248
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components legitimately shelling out to run user-authored Python tools
  • DevOps healthcheck scripts invoked by the app container calling curl/wget to internal endpoints
  • Container entrypoint wrappers where python launches bash for init tasks
  • Legitimate secrets-management tooling reading environment variables at startup
  • Security scanners/agents enumerating /etc/passwd during baselining
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","livenessProbe","readinessProbe") or ProcessCommandLine has "prometheus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent/child command line and confirm the parent is an internet-facing Langflow instance; check its version against 1.3.0 (patched). Review what the child command touched (env, /proc, files). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Langflow process, rotate any AI/cloud/DB credentials reachable from that host's environment and config. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for a new cron job beaconing every 30 min, outbound connections to 45.131.66.106 / 64.20.53.230, and any lateral SSH/MySQL auth to Nacos production servers.

| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","whoami","id","env","nc","ncat")

CVE-2025-3248 Langflow exploit — POST to /api/v1/validate/code AIDelivery High
Detects inbound exploitation of the Langflow code-validation endpoint used for JadePuffer's initial access. Any POST to /api/v1/validate/code from a non-trusted client is the exploit signature, since the endpoint passes the request body to exec() unauthenticated in vulnerable versions. Rationale: The /api/v1/validate/code path + POST verb is the exact CVE-2025-3248 exploit primitive confirmed by Zscaler/OffSec; legitimate Langflow use of this validation endpoint is rare and internal, making an external POST high-signal. Empty Defender/Falcon/CWLI/Datadog fields: this is a web-log detection with no clean endpoint-EDR or CloudTrail equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.offsec.com/blog/cve-2025-3248/ • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/cve-2025-3248-rce-vulnerability-langflow • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/security/advisories/GHSA-vwmf-pq79-vjvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Langflow developers/CI validating flow code against a self-hosted instance
  • Automated Langflow health/synthetic monitors that exercise the validate endpoint
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint during authorized scans
  • Load-balancer or WAF replaying requests for inspection
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "172.16."
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and whether it is internal/trusted; capture the request body if the WAF logs it and look for exec/decorator payloads. Check the response code — 200 suggests successful validation/execution. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, and if the Langflow build is <1.3.0 take the instance offline or gate the endpoint behind auth. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP against DeviceNetworkEvents/VPC flow, and on the Langflow host look for shell children of the python process (UC1), new cron persistence, and outbound C2 to 45.131.66.106 / 64.20.53.230.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JadePuffer C2 beaconing to 45.131.66.106 / 64.20.53.230 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two JadePuffer attacker-infrastructure IPs, which the compromised Langflow host was configured to beacon to every 30 minutes via a cron job. Pure network-IOC detection for the C2 phase. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the two attacker IPs pre-extracted from the campaign; a periodic (~30-min) beacon pattern to these IPs is the cron persistence C2 described by Sysdig. Confidence held at Medium because these IPs are currently single-source (Sysdig/BleepingComputer) — validate against ThreatFox before promoting to hard block. Datadog left empty: no generic Linux firewall/flow source in this tenant's standard Datadog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/jadepuffer-agentic-ransomware-for-automated-database-extortion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-agent-exploits-langflow-rce-to.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP re-assigned to a benign hosting tenant after takedown (stale IOC)
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating the sample and reaching the IP
  • Threat-intel scanner or honeypot infrastructure deliberately touching the IP
  • Shared VPS/CDN range where the IP later fronts legitimate services
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the beaconing host and the cadence of connections (30-min interval = strong confirmation). Confirm whether the host runs Langflow. 2) Contain: block both IPs egress at firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and remove any cron entry invoking curl/wget to these IPs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts that contacted either IP, pivot to the Nacos/MySQL production server for CVE-2021-29441 admin creation and README_RANSOM table artifacts.

Cron persistence written by a web-server process (JadePuffer 30-min beacon) AIInstallation High
Detects the JadePuffer persistence step — a cron job installed on the Langflow host to beacon every 30 minutes. Focuses on the anomaly of a web-application/shell process (python/uvicorn) invoking crontab or writing into cron directories, rather than a legitimate admin session. Rationale: Ties the cron persistence Sysdig documented to its high-fidelity anomaly: the writer is the exploited Langflow/python service (or a shell it spawned), not an interactive admin. Datadog crontab-EXECVE is broader (parent context unreliable in auditd) so it's tier-hunting supporting signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/jadepuffer-agentic-ransomware-for-automated-database-extortion • https://hackread.com/sysdig-jadepuffer-first-agentic-ransomware-operation/
ATT&CKT1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Salt) run under a shell installing legitimate cron jobs
  • Application installers/entrypoint scripts registering their own maintenance cron
  • Admin editing crontab from within a python virtualenv shell
  • Backup agents adding scheduled snapshot jobs
  • Package post-install hooks dropping files in /etc/cron.d
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written cron entry — a `*/30` schedule invoking curl/wget/bash to an external IP is the JadePuffer beacon; check the destination against 45.131.66.106 / 64.20.53.230. 2) Contain: remove the cron entry, kill any active beacon process, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: confirm the initial Langflow RCE (UC1/UC2), rotate credentials found in the host's env/config, and check the Nacos/MySQL production server for admin creation and the README_RANSOM table.

Nacos CVE-2021-29441 auth bypass — rogue admin creation via Nacos-Server UA AIExploitation High
Detects the JadePuffer lateral/priv-esc step against Alibaba Nacos: exploitation of CVE-2021-29441 by sending the User-Agent bypass header 'Nacos-Server' to the /nacos/v1/auth/users account-creation endpoint, forging a rogue administrator without authentication. Rationale: Combines the two CVE-2021-29441 exploit primitives — the /nacos/v1/auth/users user-creation path and the identity-spoofing 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent header — which together are the documented auth-bypass signature and effectively never co-occur in benign traffic. Non-web fields empty: this is a web-log-only detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/jadepuffer-agentic-ransomware-for-automated-database-extortion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-agent-exploits-langflow-rce-to.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster nodes communicating server-to-server (internal, private-source-IP)
  • Nacos administrators creating accounts through the authenticated console
  • Vulnerability scanners fingerprinting the Nacos auth endpoint
  • Internal automation provisioning Nacos users via approved service accounts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and inspect the request parameters for the created username; the internal-only 'Nacos-Server' UA arriving from outside is the bypass tell. 2) Contain: delete any rogue Nacos admin account, block the source IP, and gate the Nacos endpoint behind network ACLs; upgrade Nacos to a fixed version. 3) Hunt: on the same server look for MySQL AES_ENCRYPT activity on config_info, dropped config_info/history tables, and a README_RANSOM table (UC6); correlate the source IP with prior Langflow compromise.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/nacos/v1/auth/users"
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Nacos-Server"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos database ransomware — AES_ENCRYPT + config_info drop + README_RANSOM table AIActions on Objectives High
Detects JadePuffer's impact stage: MySQL activity encrypting Nacos config with AES_ENCRYPT(), dropping the config_info/history tables, and creating a README_RANSOM extortion table. Targets the highly specific SQL strings in process command lines and DB logs. Rationale: Uses the campaign's uniquely specific impact artifacts — the README_RANSOM table name and AES_ENCRYPT() applied to Nacos config_info, plus the config_info/history table drop — verbatim from Sysdig. These strings essentially never appear in legitimate DBA activity, giving a near-zero-FP critical alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/jadepuffer-agentic-ransomware-for-automated-database-extortion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-agent-exploits-langflow-rce-to.html • https://www.securityweek.com/agentic-ai-used-to-conduct-ransomware-attack-via-langflow/
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA legitimately using AES_ENCRYPT() for column-level encryption in an application schema (unlikely to also touch config_info)
  • A restore/migration script that drops and recreates config_info/history during a Nacos upgrade
  • Penetration test / breach-and-attack-simulation replaying the JadePuffer payload
  • Backup tooling naming a table with 'README' coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nacos-upgrade","flyway","liquibase") or ProcessCommandLine has "--dry-run")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full SQL/command line and confirm the target is a Nacos config store; verify whether config_info/history still exist and whether a README_RANSOM table now holds a BTC address + Proton Mail contact. 2) Contain: freeze the MySQL instance, preserve binlogs for forensics, do NOT pay (Sysdig confirms the AES key is random and never stored — decryption is impossible), and restore config_info/history from backup. 3) Hunt: trace back to the CVE-2021-29441 admin creation and the Langflow entry point; rotate all DB/root credentials and audit every Nacos-managed service for tampered configuration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "README_RANSOM"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "AES_ENCRYPT" and ProcessCommandLine has "config_info")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "DROP" and ProcessCommandLine has "config_info" and ProcessCommandLine has "history")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "README_RANSOM"
    or (SyslogMessage has "AES_ENCRYPT" and SyslogMessage has "config_info")
    or (SyslogMessage has "DROP" and SyslogMessage has "config_info" and SyslogMessage has "history")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nacos MySQL Ransomware Encryption and README_RANSOM Table
id: e6c1b4a7-3f92-4d0b-9a71-5c8d2e1f0b77
description: Detects JadePuffer database ransomware SQL (AES_ENCRYPT on config_info, dropping config_info/history, README_RANSOM extortion table).

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*README_RANSOM*" OR (Processes.process="*AES_ENCRYPT*" AND Processes.process="*config_info*") OR (Processes.process="*DROP*" AND Processes.process="*config_info*" AND Processes.process="*history*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
