LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ARToken/EvilTokens invoice-lure phish delivered with look-alike SharePoint / Workers IOC URL · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Successful Entra device-code authentication (EvilTokens/ARToken MFA bypass) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra device registration by a user who just completed device-code auth (PRT persistence) · [LLM] Malicious inbox rule that hides/deletes/forwards mail (ARToken BEC evidence suppression)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint egress/DNS to ARToken phishing domains and {uuid}-service.workers.dev hosts · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk SharePoint/OneDrive download fan-out after M365 account takeover (ARToken data theft) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ARToken/EvilTokens invoice-lure phish delivered with look-alike SharePoint / Workers IOC URL AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound invoice-themed emails whose embedded URL resolves to an ARToken/EvilTokens phishing host (fixed IOC domains or the {uuid}-service.workers.dev pattern) instead of the SharePoint address the message displays. Article-specific because it keys on the corroborated Talos/Sekoia infrastructure used to lure accounts-payable staff into the device-code page. Rationale: Uses the exact ARToken/EvilTokens phishing domains pre-extracted from the article and corroborated by Cisco Talos (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) plus the Talos-documented {uuid}-document/docviewer/onedrive/adobe2.workers.dev Cloudflare Workers pattern; inbound + IOC-URL is near-zero FP. Sentinel left empty because per-URL email telemetry (EmailUrlInfo/UrlClickEvents) has no clean equivalent in the tenant's Sentinel tables — the network-layer IOC UC covers Sentinel. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness/phishing-simulation platform sending test lures with look-alike URLs
  • Analyst re-sending a captured phishing sample internally for triage
  • A workers.dev subdomain used legitimately by a SaaS vendor that happens to match the -onedrive/-document suffix
  • Threat-intel newsletter or vendor advisory that quotes the IOC domain in an email body
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishingsimvendor.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the recipient is in an accounts-payable/finance role and whether DeliveryAction=Delivered vs Junked; pull the full URL and the SenderMailFromDomain (impersonated vendor). 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message from all recipient mailboxes (ZAP), block the sender domain and the IOC URL/domain at the mail gateway and web proxy, and check UrlClickEvents for any click-through. 3) Hunt: if clicked, pivot the clicking user into the device-code sign-in UC and the Entra device-registration UC to see whether a token was issued and a PRT established.

Successful Entra device-code authentication (EvilTokens/ARToken MFA bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins that used the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (device code flow) — the exact technique EvilTokens/ARToken abuse to have Microsoft issue tokens directly to the attacker while the victim completes MFA on the legitimate login page. Device code auth is rare in most tenants, so a successful one is high-signal. Rationale: AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" with ResultType==0 is the canonical detection Sekoia and Talos publish for EvilTokens/ARToken; it is a real SigninLogs column even though absent from the abbreviated schema sample here. Defender's AADSignInEventsBeta lacks that column, so it pivots on the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (appId 29d9ed98-...) that the Talos-documented clientMode:"broker" request abuses to obtain a PRT. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://research.eye.security/device-code-phishing-forensics/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in for IoT/kiosk or PowerShell/Az CLI logins in orgs that permit it
  • Help-desk assisted enrollment using device code on shared/headless devices
  • Conditional Access testing by identity admins
  • Automation using device_code grant for a service that lacks a browser
Suppression filter
| where UserPrincipalName !in~ ("svc-kiosk@contoso.com", "iot-enroll@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the org legitimately uses device-code flow at all; inspect the sign-in's IPAddress/Country/ResourceDisplayName and whether the same user has a concurrent interactive sign-in from a different geo. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset + re-MFA, and add a Conditional Access policy blocking the device-code flow for non-exempt users. 3) Hunt: pivot the user into the device-registration UC (T1098.005) and the inbox-rule UC to catch PRT persistence and BEC track-covering.
// AADSignInEventsBeta has no AuthenticationProtocol column, so pivot on the device-code -> PRT app: Microsoft Authentication Broker (clientMode:broker per Talos)
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"
    | summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker — mints the PRT
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Country
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, DeviceTrustType, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode"   // canonical Sekoia/Talos device-code indicator
| where ResultType == 0                          // successful token issuance only
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(LocationDetails).countryOrRegion)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20) by UserPrincipalName
| order by FirstSeen desc

CLOUD

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Authentication.app) as app values(Authentication.src) as src min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.signature="deviceCode" by Authentication.user

Entra device registration by a user who just completed device-code auth (PRT persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a successful device-code sign-in with a subsequent 'Add/Register device' in Entra ID by the same user — the exact PRT-persistence chain (/prt/setup, /prt/refresh, /prt/renew, /prt/reacquire) EvilTokens/ARToken use to register an attacker device and silently mint Primary Refresh Tokens that survive password resets. Rationale: Talos documents the /prt/setup, /prt/refresh, /prt/renew and /prt/reacquire persistence chain and the clientMode:"broker" device registration; joining a deviceCode sign-in to a same-user device-registration audit event isolates that PRT chain from routine Intune enrollments. Sigma skipped because the detection is a cross-table (SigninLogs x AuditLogs) correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Intune / Autopilot device enrollment following a legitimate device-code login on a new laptop
  • BYOD registration by a remote user connecting from a home/mobile IP
  • Identity admin bulk-registering devices during a migration
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning that registers the device
Suppression filter
| where ActorIP != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the registered device's join IP/country to the user's usual sign-in geo and confirm the device name isn't standard corporate naming; check for a device-code sign-in minutes earlier. 2) Contain: disable/delete the rogue device object in Entra, revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, and reset credentials (a PRT survives password reset alone). 3) Hunt: query all recent devices registered by finance/AP users and pivot to inbox-rule creation and bulk mailbox/SharePoint access from the same actor.
// A newly-registered device authenticating = candidate attacker device holding a PRT
let KnownDevices = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where isnotempty(AadDeviceId)
    | summarize by AccountUpn, AadDeviceId;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD registered"
| join kind=leftanti KnownDevices on AccountUpn, AadDeviceId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AadDeviceId, DeviceName, DeviceTrustType, IPAddress, Country, City, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeUsers = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" and ResultType == 0
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Add device", "Register device", "Add registered owner to device")
| where Result == "success"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where Actor in (DeviceCodeUsers)
| extend TargetDevice = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIP, TargetDevice, TargetResources
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| sort - firstTime
Malicious inbox rule that hides/deletes/forwards mail (ARToken BEC evidence suppression) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation/modification of Outlook inbox rules that delete, mark-as-read, move to Deleted Items/RSS, or auto-forward/redirect messages — the exact ARToken ARTSender capability for BEC evidence suppression and silent thread hijacking after account takeover. Rationale: Talos explicitly describes ARTSender creating inbox rules for 'forwarding and auto-deletion (evidence suppression)'; keying on DeleteMessage/MoveToFolder-to-Deleted-Items/ForwardTo in New-/Set-InboxRule parameters isolates the malicious rules from benign organizational rules. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because O365 mailbox-rule audit is not shipped to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User creating a legitimate rule to auto-file newsletters into a folder
  • Out-of-office / delegate rule forwarding to a manager or shared mailbox
  • Admin-deployed transport/retention rules moving mail to Archive
  • Power-user organizing mail into RSS/Deleted-Items cleanup rules
Suppression filter
| where not (Params has "ForwardTo" and Operation == "New-InboxRule" and ClientIP == "")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the rule's exact conditions/actions (keyword filters on 'invoice', 'payment', 'wire', forward-to external address, move-to Deleted Items) and correlate the creator's recent sign-in for device-code/anomalous geo. 2) Contain: delete the rule, revoke the user's sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and block any external forwarding target domain. 3) Hunt: sweep all mailboxes for rules created in the same window from the same IP and pivot to bulk SharePoint/OneDrive download by that actor.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules", "Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "ForwardAsAttachmentTo", "MarkAsRead")
| where Raw has_any ("Deleted Items", "Junk", "RSS", "Archive", "DeleteMessage", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "ForwardAsAttachmentTo", "MarkAsRead")
| where Params has_any ("Deleted Items", "Junk Email", "RSS Feeds", "RSS Subscriptions", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, ObjectId, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint egress/DNS to ARToken phishing domains and {uuid}-service.workers.dev hosts AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution/connection to the ARToken/EvilTokens fixed IOC domains and to the Talos-documented Cloudflare Workers naming pattern {uuid}-document/docviewer/onedrive/adobe2.workers.dev used to serve the device-code phishing pages. Network-layer coverage for the same campaign across Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog. Rationale: Ships the corroborated ARToken C2/panel domains (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) plus all article IOC domains, and adds the Talos-documented {uuid}-document/docviewer/onedrive/adobe2.workers.dev Cloudflare Workers pattern so detection survives per-affiliate domain rotation. Endpoint DNS/connection to these is near-zero FP. Sentinel DnsEvents query projects the valid ClientIP/Name/QueryType/Result columns (not IPAddresses). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate SaaS product hosted on a workers.dev subdomain that happens to end in -onedrive/-document
  • Security researcher/analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains for verdicts
  • Web proxy pre-fetch/URL-rewrite service touching the domain on the user's behalf
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process/user that initiated (browser vs script), and check whether the resolution was followed by an Entra device-code sign-in for that user. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain and the workers.dev pattern at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a non-browser process resolved it, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: pull all hosts/users that resolved any campaign domain in 30 days and pivot each into the device-code sign-in and inbox-rule UCs.

Bulk SharePoint/OneDrive download fan-out after M365 account takeover (ARToken data theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single user/IP downloading an anomalous volume of distinct SharePoint/OneDrive files in a short window — the ARToken capability to browse and exfiltrate victims' SharePoint sites and OneDrive files (and stage malware) after token theft. Threshold-based collection detection distinct from the identity/email pivots. Rationale: The article/Talos state ARToken lets operators browse, download and manage victims' SharePoint and OneDrive files for data theft; a per-user/IP FileDownloaded fan-out over distinct files is the cleanest signal of that bulk collection. Thresholds (>100 downloads, >50 distinct files) are commented and should be tuned to the org's 90-day P99. Sigma skipped (aggregation/threshold detection). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/cisco-talos-exposes-artoken-microsoft-365-phishing-kit/
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1530
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User doing a legitimate bulk offboarding/backup export of their OneDrive
  • New employee syncing large SharePoint libraries via OneDrive client on first login
  • Migration or eDiscovery tooling downloading many files under a service/admin account
  • Data-analyst pulling a large document set for a project
Suppression filter
| where UserId !in~ ("svc-migration@contoso.com", "ediscovery@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the download volume/IP/geo to the user's baseline and check whether it followed a device-code sign-in or new device registration; inspect which sites/sensitivity-labeled files were pulled. 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and apply Conditional Access / session controls; where possible restrict download on sensitive sites. 3) Hunt: correlate to inbox-rule creation and outbound BEC mail from the same actor, and check whether any downloaded file was re-uploaded as a malware lure to other tenants.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft SharePoint Online", "Microsoft OneDrive for Business")
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(ObjectId), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName
| where Downloads > 100 and DistinctFiles > 50   // bulk-staging threshold; tune to org P99
| order by Downloads desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive")
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(ObjectId), Sites = make_set(Site_Url, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, ClientIP
| where Downloads > 100 and DistinctFiles > 50   // bulk-staging threshold; tune to org P99 (per-user 90-day baseline)
| order by Downloads desc
APPLICATION
sourcetype="o365:management:activity" (Workload=SharePoint OR Workload=OneDrive) Operation="FileDownloaded"
| stats count as downloads dc(ObjectId) as distinctFiles values(Site_Url) as sites min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by UserId ClientIP
| where downloads>100 AND distinctFiles>50
| sort - downloads
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"

| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
